If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion

If the mean of 10 observations is 50 and the sum of the squares of the deviations of the

11770.sol:
Given, number of observation, $n=10$,
Mean, $\bar{x}=50$ and $\sum|x i-\bar{x}|^2=250$
Variance, $\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\left|x_i-\bar{x}\right|^2}{n}\begin{gathered}
\Rightarrow \sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^{10} \frac{\left|x_i-\bar{x}^2\right|}{10} \\
=\frac{250}{10}=25 \Rightarrow \sigma=5
\end{gathered}\therefore$ Cofficient of variation,
$\text{ C.V. }=\frac{\sigma}{x} \times 100=\frac{5}{50} \times 100=10$

13313.text: If $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are coterminous edges of $\mathbf{a}$ parallelopiped such that $\left|$\begin{array}{lll}$\mathbf{a}$ \cdot $\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{a}$ \cdot $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{a}$ \cdot $\mathbf{c}$ \\ $\mathbf{b}$ \cdot $\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ \cdot $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ \cdot $\mathbf{c}$ \\ $\mathbf{c}$ \cdot $\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{c}$ \cdot $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$ \cdot $\mathbf{c}$\end{array}$\right|=16$, then find the volume of the parallelopiped

It is given that, $\left|\begin{array}{lll}\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} & \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} & \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} \\ \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a} & \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b} & \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c} \\ \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a} & \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b} & \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c}\end{array}\right|=16$

$\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}$& $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b}$& $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}$\\
$\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}$& $\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b}$& $\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c}
\end{array}\right|$\\
& =$\left\lvert$\, $\begin{array}{cc}$ a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2 & a_1 b_1+a_2 b_2+a_3 b_3 \\
b_1 a_1+b_2 a_2+b_3 a_3 & b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2 \\
c_1 a_1+c_2 a_2+c_3 a_3 & c_1 b_1+c_2 b_2+c_3 b_3
\end{array}\right. \\
& a_1 c_1+a_2 c_2+a_3 c_3 \\
& b_1 c_1+b_2 c_2+b_3 c_3 \\
& c_1^2+c_2^2+c_3^2 \\
&
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned}$& =$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\
b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\
c_1 & c_2 & c_3
\end{array}\right|$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\
a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\
a_3 & b_3 & c_3
\end{array}\right| \\
& =$\left[\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{a}$& $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$
\end{array}\right]$\left[\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{a}$& $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$
\end{array}\right]=16 \\
& \therefore \quad$\left[\begin{array}{lll}
\mathbf{a}$& $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$
\end{array}\right]=4 \\
&
\end{aligned}

(given)

So, the volume of the parallelopiped having coterminous edges is 4.

17201.text: A man who is running has half the kinetic energy of a boy of half his mass. The man speeds up by \(1 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}\) and then has the same kinetic energy as the boy. The initial speed of the boy is
17201.sol:
According to the question, let the mass of man be \(m\).
So, mass of boy is \(\frac{m}{2}\).
Let speed of man be \(v_1\) and that of boy be \(v_2\).
\(\therefore\) Kinetic energy of man \(=\frac{1}{2}\) kinetic energy of boy
or \(\mathrm{KE}_{\operatorname{man}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{KE}_{\text{boy }}\)
\(\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{m}{2} v_2^2 \text{ or } \frac{v_1^2}{v_2^2}=\frac{1}{4}\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad \frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{1}{2}\)
\(\therefore \quad v_1=\frac{1}{2} v_2\)...(i)
If the velocity of man increased by \(1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\) then, new velocity of man, \(v_1^{\prime}=\left(\frac{v_2}{2}+1\right)[\therefore\) From Eq. (i)]
Now, kinetic energy of man (KE) = kinetic energy of Boy \(\left(\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\)
\(\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \frac{1}{2} \times m \times\left(\frac{v_2}{2}+1\right)^2 & =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{m}{2} \times v_2^2 \\
\left(\frac{v_2}{2}+1\right)^2 & =\left(\frac{v_2}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \\
\frac{v_2}{2}+1 & =\frac{v_2}{\sqrt{2}} \\
\sqrt{2} v_2+2 \sqrt{2} & =2 v_2 \\
2 \sqrt{2} & =2 v_2-\sqrt{2} v_2 \\
\sqrt{2} v_2(\sqrt{2}-1) & =2 \sqrt{2} \\
v_2= & \frac{2}{(\sqrt{2}-1)} \\
v_2= & \frac{2}{(\sqrt{2}-1)} \times \frac{(\sqrt{2}+1)}{(\sqrt{2}+1)}=\frac{2(\sqrt{2}+1)}{(2-1)} \\
v_2= & 2(\sqrt{2}+1)
\end{aligned}\)
So, the initial speed of the boy, \(v_2=2(\sqrt{2}+1)\).

19911.subject: Chemistry
19911.text:
For a reaction, $2 A+B \longrightarrow$ products,
If concentration of $B$ is kept constant and concentration of $A$ is doubled then rate of reaction is
19911.sol:
The rate law for a reaction $2A + B \rightarrow$ products is given by the expression $Rate = k[A]^{x}[B]^{y}$, where $x$ and $y$ are the orders of reaction with respect to A$ and $B$ respectively.

Given that the reaction is 2A + B \rightarrow$ products, the order with respect to A$ is 2$ based on the stoichiometry of the elementary reaction.

The rate expression becomes $Rate = k[A]^{2}[B]^{y}$.

When the concentration of A$ is doubled, let the new concentration be $[A'] = 2[A]$. The concentration of $B$ is kept constant.

The new rate $Rate'$ is given by $Rate' = k(2[A])^{2}[B]^{y} = k(4[A]^{2})[B]^{y} = 4 \times k[A]^{2}[B]^{y} = 4 \times Rate$.

Therefore, the rate of the reaction is quadrupled.

Answer: quadrupled$

20670.subject: Chemistry
20670.text: $\mathrm{X}$ is an electrolyte with a concentration of $0.04 \mathrm{M}$ whose formula is of the type $\mathrm{X}_2 \mathrm{ A}$. $\mathrm{Y}$ is a non-electrolyte solution with a concentration of $0.2 \mathrm{M}$ and has an osmotic pressure equal to $\mathrm{P}_2$ at room temperature. What is the relationship between the Osmotic pressure $\pi$ of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{P}_2$ ?
20670.sol:
The osmotic pressure $\pi$ of a solution is given by the formula $\pi = iCRT$, where $i$ is the van't Hoff factor, $C$ is the molar concentration, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature.

For the electrolyte $X_2A$, it dissociates as $X_2A \rightarrow 2X^{+} + A^{2-}$. The number of ions produced per formula unit is $n = 3$. Assuming complete dissociation, the van't Hoff factor $i = 3$. Given $C_X = 0.04 \text{ M}$, the osmotic pressure $\pi$ is $\pi = 3 \times 0.04 \times RT = 0.12 RT$.

For the non-electrolyte $Y$, the van't Hoff factor $i = 1$. Given $C_Y = 0.2 \text{ M}$, the osmotic pressure $P_2$ is $P_2 = 1 \times 0.2 \times RT = 0.2 RT$.

To find the relationship between $\pi$ and $P_2$, we take the ratio $\dfrac{\pi}{P_2} = \dfrac{0.12 RT}{0.2 RT} = \dfrac{0.12}{0.2} = 0.6$.

Therefore, $\pi = 0.6 P_2$.

Answer: $\pi=0.6 P_2$

Given the differential equation $f(x) = f'(x)$, we can write it as $\dfrac{df}{dx} = f(x)$.

22365.text: The instantaneous values of alternating current and voltages in a circuit are $I=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \sin (200 \pi t)$ ampere and $\mathrm{V}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \sin \left(200 \pi t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ volt. What is the average power consumed in the circuit in watt?
22365.sol:
The given expressions for current and voltage are $I = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(200 \pi t)$ and $V = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \sin(200 \pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{6})$.

The peak current is $I_0 = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$ A and the peak voltage is $V_0 = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$ V.

The root mean square values are $I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ A and $V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ V.

The phase difference between voltage and current is $\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

The average power consumed in an AC circuit is given by $P_{avg} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \phi$.

Substituting the values, $P_{avg} = \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right) \times \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)$.

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{9}{4} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8}$ W.

Answer: $\dfrac{9 \sqrt{3}}{8}$

22577.subject: Physics
22577.text: Two wires A and B made of same material having length 10 cm and 40 cm respectively are connected in parallel to the same source of emf 10 V. What will be the ratio of the drift velocity of the electrons in the wire $A$ to the drift velocity in the wire $B$ ?
22577.sol:
The drift velocity $v_{d}$ of electrons in a conductor is given by the formula $v_{d} = \dfrac{I}{neA}$, where $I$ is the current, $n$ is the electron density, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area. Since the wires are made of the same material, $n$ is the same for both.

The current $I$ in a wire is given by $I = \dfrac{V}{R}$, where $V$ is the potential difference and $R$ is the resistance. The resistance $R$ is given by $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is the resistivity and $l$ is the length. Substituting this into the expression for current, $I = \dfrac{VA}{\rho l}$.

Substituting $I$ into the drift velocity formula, $v_{d} = \dfrac{VA}{neA\rho l} = \dfrac{V}{ne\rho l}$.

Since both wires are connected to the same source of emf, $V$ is the same for both. The material is the same, so $n$ and $\rho$ are constant. Therefore, $v_{d} \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$.

The ratio of drift velocities is $\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}} = \dfrac{l_{B}}{l_{A}}$.

Given $l_{A} = 10$ cm and $l_{B} = 40$ cm, we have $\dfrac{v_{dA}}{v_{dB}} = \dfrac{40}{10} = \dfrac{4}{1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{V_{d A}}{V_{d B}}=4: 1$

22922.text: The height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\dfrac{g}{16}$ (where, $g=$ acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth) in terms of $R$ is, if $R$ is the radius of earth.
22922.sol:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the earth is given by the formula $g_h = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R + h} \right)^2$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and $R$ is the radius of the earth.

Given that $g_h = \dfrac{g}{16}$, we substitute this into the equation:

$\dfrac{g}{16} = g \left( \dfrac{R}{R + h} \right)^2$

Dividing both sides by $g$ and taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{R}{R + h}$

Cross-multiplying gives:

$R + h = 4R$

$h = 3R$

Answer: $3 R$

23043.subject: Physics
23043.text: An electric current $I$ enters and leaves a uniform circular wire of radius $r$ through diametrically opposite points. A charged particle $q$ moves along the axis of circular wire passes through its centre with speed $v$. The magnetic force on the particle when it passes through the centre has a magnitude
23043.sol:
The circular wire is divided into two semi-circular segments by the diametrically opposite points where the current enters and leaves. Let the current $I$ split into $I_1$ and $I_2$ through the two semi-circular paths. Since the wire is uniform, the resistance of each semi-circular path is equal, so $I_1 = I_2 = I/2$.

The magnetic field $B_1$ at the center due to the first semi-circular wire carrying current $I/2$ is directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Using the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field at the center of a full circular loop is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$. For a semi-circular wire, the field is half of this, $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 (I/2)}{4r} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$.

The magnetic field $B_2$ at the center due to the second semi-circular wire carrying current $I/2$ is also $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$, but its direction is opposite to that of $B_1$ because the current flows in the opposite sense relative to the center. Thus, the net magnetic field $B_{net} = B_1 - B_2 = 0$.

The magnetic force on a charged particle moving with velocity $v$ is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} imes \vec{B})$. Since the net magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at the center is zero, the magnetic force on the particle is $F = q v (0) = 0$.

Answer: 0

26488.subject: Physics
26488.text: A spring - block system is resting on a frictionless floor as shown in the figure. The spring constant is $2.0N{m}^{- 1}$ and the mass of the block is $2.0kg$ . Ignore the mass of the spring. Initially the spring is in an unstretched condition. Another block of mass 1.0kg moving with a speed of $2.0m{s}^{- 1}$ collides elastically with the first block. The collision is such that the 2.0kg block does not hit the wall. The distance, in metres, between the two blocks when the spring returns to its unstretched position for the first time after the collision is _________.
26488.sol:
Given here: $m = 2 . 0kg$ and $k = 2 . 0N{m}^{- 1}$.

Time period of spring is given as $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pisec$
Block returns to original position in $\dfrac{T}{2} = \pisec$

The speed of block after collision is $v = \dfrac{2 \times 2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{4}{3}m / s$ and $v ' = \dfrac{2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{2}{3}m / s$.

The distance between the two blocks is $d = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\pi\right) = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(3.14\right) = 2.0933m$
$d = 2.09m$

26682.text:
Answer the following by appropriately matching the lists based on the information given in the paragraph.
In a thermodynamics process on an ideal monatomic gas, the infinitesimal heat absorbed by the gas is given by $T\DeltaX,$ where $T$ is temperature of the system and $\DeltaX$ is the infinitesimal change in a thermodynamic quantity $X$ of the system. For a mole of monatomic ideal gas $X = \dfrac{3}{2}Rln\left(\dfrac{T}{{T}_{A}}\right) + Rln\left(\dfrac{V}{{V}_{A}}\right) .$ Here, $R$ is gas constant, $V$ is volume of gas, ${T}_{A}$ and ${V}_{A}$ are constants.
The List-I below gives some quantities involved in a process and List-II gives some possible values of these quantities.
 

 List I List II
$( a )$Work done by the system in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( p )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}ln2$
$( b )$Change in internal energy in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( q )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}$
$( c )$Heat absorbed by the system in process $1 \to 2 \to 3$$( r )$$R{T}_{0}$
$( d )$Heat absorbed by the system in process $1 \to 2$$( s )$$\dfrac{4}{3}R{T}_{0}$
  $( t )$$\dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0}\left(3 + ln2\right)$
  $( u )$$\dfrac{5}{6}R{T}_{0}$

If the process carried out on one mole of monatomic ideal gas is as shown in figure in the $T$ - $V$ -diagram with ${P}_{0}{V}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{3}R{T}_{0},$ the correct match is,
options: $a - q, b - r, c - p, d - u$
$a - s, b - r, c - q, d - t$
$a - q, b - r, c - s, d - u$
$a - p, b - r, c - t, d - p$
26682.sol:
$1$ - $2$ process is isothermal and $2$ - $3$ process is isochoric.
$\left(a\right){W}_{1 \to 2} = nRTln\dfrac{{V}_{f}}{{F}_{i}} = 1 \times R\dfrac{{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{V}_{1}} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ \dfrac{2{V}_{0}}{{V}_{0}} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2$
${W}_{2 \to 3} = 0$ (isochoric process)
${W}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = {W}_{1 \to 2} + {W}_{2 \to 3} = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2\left(a \to P\right)$
$\left(b\right) ∆ U = \dfrac{f}{2}nR\left({T}_{f} - {T}_{i}\right)$
$∆ {U}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = \dfrac{3}{2}\left[1 \times R\left({T}_{0} - \dfrac{{T}_{0}}{3}\right)\right]$
$\begin{cases}= R{T}_{0} & \left(b \to R\right)\end{cases}$
$\left(c\right){Q}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} = ∆ {U}_{1 \to 2 \to 3} + {W}_{1 \to 2 \to 3}$ (First law of thermodynamics)
$= R{T}_{0} + \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2$
$\begin{cases}= \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}\left[3 + ln ⁡ 2\right] & \left(c \to t\right)\end{cases}$
$\left(d\right){Q}_{1 \to 2} = ∆ {U}_{1 \to 2} + {W}_{1 \to 2}$
$\begin{cases}= 0 + \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2 = \dfrac{R{T}_{0}}{3}ln ⁡ 2 & \left(d \to p\right)\end{cases}$

29297.text: Consider the following electrochemical cell : $\mathrm{Pt}\left|\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{ g})(1 \mathrm{bar})\right| \mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq}) \| \mathrm{M}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}, 1.0 \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{M}(\mathrm{ s})$ The pH above which, oxygen gas would start to evolve at anode is $\_\_\_\_$ (nearest integer).  $\left[$\begin{array}{ll}$\text{ Given: }$ & $\mathrm{E}^{\mathrm{o}$}{ }_{$\mathrm{M}^{2+}$ / $\mathrm{M}$}=0.994 $\mathrm{ V}$ \\ & $\mathrm{E}^{\mathrm{o}$}{ }_{$\mathrm{O}_{2}$ / $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$}=1.23 $\mathrm{ V}$\end{array}$\right\}$ standard reduction potential ]
29297.sol:
In this electrochemical cell, at the anode oxygen evolution occurs from water oxidation. Using Nernst equation for the O₂/H₂O couple: $E_{anode} = E°_{O_2/H_2O} - \frac{0.059}{4} \log \frac{1}{[H^+]^4} = 1.23 - 0.059 \times pH$

At the cathode: $E_{cathode} = 0.994$ V (standard potential for M²⁺/M reduction)

For oxygen to start evolving, the cell potential becomes zero: $E_{cell} = E_{cathode} - E_{anode} = 0$

$0.994 = 1.23 - 0.059 \times pH$

$0.059 \times pH = 0.236$

$pH = 4.0$

29648.subject: Chemistry
29648.text: CORRECT order of stability for the following is $\mathrm{CH}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}^{-}, \mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}^{-}, \mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{C}^{-}$
29648.sol:
Carbanion stability is determined by the s-character of the hybrid orbital bearing the negative charge.
The acetylide anion $CH \equiv C^-$ has the carbanion on an sp hybridized carbon (50% s-character), providing optimal stabilization through efficient overlap with the charged orbital.
The vinyl anion $CH_2 = CH^-$ has the carbanion on an sp² hybridized carbon (33% s-character), offering moderate stabilization.
The primary alkyl anion $CH_3 - CH_2^-$ has the carbanion on an sp³ hybridized carbon (25% s-character), providing the least stabilization.
Greater s-character enables better penetration of the nucleus and enhanced stabilization of the negative charge.
Therefore, the order is $CH \equiv C^- > CH_2 = CH^- > CH_3 - CH_2^-$.

30981.subject: Chemistry
30981.text:
Given below are two statements :
Statement (I) : Oxidising power of halogens decreases in the order $F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2$, which is the basis of "Layer test".
Statement (II) : "Layer test" to identify $Br_2$ and $I_2$ in aqueous solution involves the oxidation of bromide or iodide into $Br_2$ or $I_2$ respectively with $Cl_2$, which is a type of displacement redox reaction.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
30981.sol:
Statement I is true. The oxidising power of halogens decreases down the group in the order $F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2$. A stronger oxidising halogen can displace a weaker oxidising halogen from its aqueous halide solution. This principle forms the basis of the layer test.

Statement II is true. In the layer test, chlorine water ($Cl_2$) is added to an aqueous solution containing bromide ($Br^-$) or iodide ($I^-$) ions. Since $Cl_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent, it oxidises $Br^-$ to $Br_2$ and $I^-$ to $I_2$. The reaction is given by:
$Cl_2 + 2X^- \rightarrow 2Cl^- + X_2$ (where $X = Br, I$)
This is a non-metal displacement redox reaction. The liberated $Br_2$ or $I_2$ is then extracted into an organic solvent layer (like $CHCl_3$ or $CCl_4$), where it imparts a characteristic orange-red colour for $Br_2$ or a violet colour for $I_2$, thereby identifying them.

Therefore, both Statement I and Statement II are true.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

32079.text: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen contains $40 %$ hydrogen by mass when the pressure is $2 . 2$ bar. The partial pressure of hydrogen is bar.

According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, the total pressure by a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of each of the constituent gases.

${P}_{i} = {x}_{i}P{P}_{i} = partialpressureof{i}^{th}component . {x}_{i} = molefractionofthe{i}^{th}componentP = totalpressure$

${P}_{{H}_{2}} = \left(\dfrac{20}{20 + \dfrac{15}{8}}\right) \times 2 . 2$

$= \dfrac{20}{20 + 1 . 875} \times 2 . 2$

$= \dfrac{20}{21 . 875} \times 2 . 2$

$= 2 . 0114$

32834.text: The set of all $a \in \mathbb{R}$ for which the equation $x | x - 1 | + | x + 2 | + a = 0$ has exactly one real root, is
32834.sol:
Given,

$x | x - 1 | + | x + 2 | + a = 0$

Now taking, Case I: $x < - 2$, we get

$- {x}^{2} + x - x - 2 + a = 0$

$⇒ a = {x}^{2} + 2$

And $y = {x}^{2} + 2$ is decreasing $∀ x \in ( - \infty , - 2 )$

Now taking Case II: $- 2 \le x < 1$ we get,

$- {x}^{2} + x + x + 2 + a = 0$

$⇒ a = {x}^{2} - 2x - 2$

And $y = {x}^{2} - 2x - 2$

So, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x - 1 \le 0 ∀ x \in [ - 2, 1 )$

Hence, $y$ is decreasing $∀ x \in [ - 2, 1 )$

34818.text: If ${x}^{3}dy + xy \cdot dx = {x}^{2}dy + 2ydx; y\left(2\right) = e$ and $x > 1$, then $y\left(4\right)$ is equal to :
34818.sol:
Given ${x}^{3}dy + xy \cdot dx = {x}^{2}dy + 2ydx$

$⇒ \left({x}^{3} - {x}^{2}\right)dy = \left(2 - x\right)ydx$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{y} = \dfrac{\left(2 - x\right)}{\left({x}^{3} - {x}^{2}\right)}dx$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

$∫ \dfrac{dy}{y} = ∫ \dfrac{\left(2 - x\right)}{{x}^{2}\left(x - 1\right)}dx + k . . . . . . . . . . . . \left(i\right)$

Let $\dfrac{\left(2 - x\right)}{{x}^{2}\left(x - 1\right)} = \dfrac{A}{x} + \dfrac{B}{{x}^{2}} + \dfrac{C}{\left(x - 1\right)}$

$⇒ \left(2 - x\right) = Ax\left(x - 1\right) + B\left(x - 1\right) + C{x}^{2}$

Putting $x = 0 ⇒ 2 = - B ⇒ B = - 2$

Putting $x = 1 ⇒ 2 - 1 = C ⇒ C = 1$

Putting $x = 2 ⇒ 2 - 2 = A\left(2\right)\left(1\right) + B\left(1\right) + C\left({2}^{2}\right) ⇒ 2A + 2 = 0 ⇒ A = - 1$

From equation $\left(i\right)$, we get

$∫ \dfrac{dy}{y} = ∫ \left(\dfrac{- 1}{x} + \dfrac{- 2}{{x}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{x - 1}\right)dx + k$

$⇒ lny = - lnx + \dfrac{2}{x} + ln\left|x - 1\right| + k . . . . . . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

Given $y\left(2\right) = e$ i.e. at $x = 2, y = e$

$⇒ lne = - ln2 + \dfrac{2}{2} + ln\left|2 - 1\right| + k$

$⇒ 1 = - ln2 + 1 + 0 + k$

$⇒ k = ln2$

Putting in equation $\left(ii\right)$, we get

$lny = - lnx + \dfrac{2}{x} + ln\left|x - 1\right| + ln2$

Now putting $x = 4$, we get

$lny = - ln4 + \dfrac{2}{4} + ln\left|4 - 1\right| + ln2$

$⇒ lny = - 2ln2 + \dfrac{1}{2} + ln3 + ln2$

$⇒ lny = - ln2 + \dfrac{1}{2} + ln3$

$⇒ lny = \dfrac{1}{2} + ln\dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ ln\dfrac{2y}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2y}{3} = e\dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{e}$

$⇒ y\left(4\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{e}$

36175.subject: Mathematics
36175.text: Let O be the vertex of the parabola $y^2=4x$ and its chords OP and OQ are perpendicular to each other. If the locus of the mid-point of the line segment PQ is a conic C, then the length of its latus rectum is:
36175.sol:
Let the vertex of the parabola $y^2 = 4x$ be $O(0, 0)$.

Let the coordinates of the points $P$ and $Q$ on the parabola be $(t_1^2, 2t_1)$ and $(t_2^2, 2t_2)$ respectively.

The slope of the chord $OP$ is $m_1 = \dfrac{2t_1 - 0}{t_1^2 - 0} = \dfrac{2}{t_1}$.

The slope of the chord $OQ$ is $m_2 = \dfrac{2t_2 - 0}{t_2^2 - 0} = \dfrac{2}{t_2}$.

Since $OP$ and $OQ$ are perpendicular to each other, $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

$\Rightarrow \left(\dfrac{2}{t_1}\right) \left(\dfrac{2}{t_2}\right) = -1$

$\Rightarrow t_1 t_2 = -4$

Let $M(h, k)$ be the mid-point of the line segment $PQ$. Then,

$h = \dfrac{t_1^2 + t_2^2}{2} \Rightarrow t_1^2 + t_2^2 = 2h$

$k = \dfrac{2t_1 + 2t_2}{2} \Rightarrow t_1 + t_2 = k$

Squaring the equation for $k$, we get:

$k^2 = (t_1 + t_2)^2 = t_1^2 + t_2^2 + 2t_1 t_2$

Substituting the values of $t_1^2 + t_2^2$ and $t_1 t_2$, we obtain:

$k^2 = 2h + 2(-4)$

$k^2 = 2h - 8$

$k^2 = 2(h - 4)$

Replacing $h$ with $x$ and $k$ with $y$, the locus of the mid-point is:

$y^2 = 2(x - 4)$

This represents a parabola of the form $Y^2 = 4AX$, where the length of the latus rectum is $4A = 2$.

Answer: $2$

42655.subject: Physics
42655.text: The frequency of oscillation of a mass $m$ suspended by a spring is $v_1$. If the length of the spring is cut to half, the same mass oscillates with frequency $v_2$. The value of $v_2/v_1$ is ________.
42655.sol:
The frequency of oscillation of a spring-mass system is given by $v = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$, where $k$ is the spring constant and $m$ is the mass.

The spring constant $k$ is inversely proportional to the length of the spring $L$, so $k \propto \dfrac{1}{L}$.

When the length of the spring is cut to half, the new length is $L' = \dfrac{L}{2}$. The new spring constant becomes $k' = 2k$.

The new frequency of oscillation is $v_2 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{k'}{m}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\dfrac{2k}{m}} = \sqrt{2} v_1$.

Therefore, the ratio $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{2}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}$

\frac{d y}{d x}$& =$\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\left(\frac{2}{\pi}+0\right)+1 $\cdot($0+0)=1
\end{aligned}
$

49577.sol:
We know that, $\cos 2 \alpha=2 \cos ^{2} \alpha-1$
So, $\cos 2 \alpha+\cos 2 \beta+\cos 2 \gamma=2\left(\cos ^{2} \alpha+\cos ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \gamma\right)-3$

Therefore,
$\cos 2 \alpha+\cos 2 \beta+\cos 2 \gamma=2(1)-3=-1$

55653.subject: Chemistry
55653.text: Identify the reason for the highest boiling point of R-COOH as compared to alkanes, ethers, alcohols and aldehydes.
options: Van der waals force of attraction
55653.sol:
Carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alkanes, ethers, alcohols, and aldehydes of comparable molecular mass.

This is due to the presence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding in carboxylic acids. The highly polarized O-H bond, enhanced by the electron-withdrawing carbonyl group, allows carboxylic acid molecules to form strong hydrogen bonds with each other. Because of this extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding, they often exist as dimers even in the vapor phase or in non-polar solvents, requiring more energy to separate the molecules during boiling.

Answer: Formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonding

56044.text: Rate law for the reaction $\mathrm{aA}+\mathrm{bB} \rightarrow \mathrm{cC}+\mathrm{dD}$ is $\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$, the rate of reaction doubles if
options: Concentration of both $A$ and $B$ are doubled.
Concentration of $A$ is doubled and concentration of $B$ is kept constant.
Concentration of $B$ is doubled and concentration of $A$ is halved.
Concentration of A is kept constant and concentration of B is halved.
56044.sol:
The rate law is given as $r = k[A][B]$ for the reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$.

The initial rate is $r_1 = k[A][B]$.

To double the rate, we require $r_2 = 2r_1 = 2k[A][B]$.

When concentration $A$ is doubled while $B$ remains constant, the new rate becomes $k(2[A])([B]) = 2k[A][B]$.

This matches the required doubling condition, confirming option B is correct.

Other options yield different results: doubling both concentrations quadruples the rate, doubling $B$ while halving $A$ maintains the original rate, and halving $B$ while keeping $A$ constant halves the rate.

57578.subject: Chemistry
57578.text: Which of the following is a correct feature of the $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism?
options: The $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism proceeds mainly with racemization.
The $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism includes a transition state with penta coordinating carbon.
The $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism involves formation of planar carbocation intermediate in the first step.
The $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism involves formation of carbocation with $\text{SP}^2$ hybridized carbon.
57578.sol:
The $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ mechanism is a concerted, single-step process where the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group.

During this process, a transition state is formed in which the central carbon atom is partially bonded to five groups (the incoming nucleophile, the leaving group, and three other substituents), making it penta-coordinated.

There is no carbocation intermediate formed in the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ mechanism, which rules out the formation of a planar $\text{sp}^2$ hybridized carbocation.

The reaction proceeds with complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), not racemization.

Answer: The $\text{SN}^2$ mechanism includes a transition state with penta coordinating carbon.

57982.text: Identify the strongest base according to Bronsted-Lowry theory from following.
57982.sol:
According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory, a stronger base has a weaker conjugate acid.

The conjugate acids of the given bases are:
$\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{HCl}$ (strong acid)
$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (weak acid)
$\text{NO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3$ (strong acid)
$\text{HSO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (strong acid)

Since $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is the weakest acid among the given conjugate acids, its conjugate base $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ is the strongest base.

Answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$

59781.subject: Chemistry
59781.text: Which from following represents the Freundlich's empirical equation for adsorption of gas on solid (for $\mathrm{n} > 1$)
59781.sol:
The Freundlich adsorption isotherm provides an empirical relationship describing the amount of gas adsorbed per unit mass of solid adsorbent in terms of pressure at a fixed temperature, expressed as

$\frac{x}{m} = kP^{\frac{1}{n}}$

where $x$ is the mass of the adsorbate, $m$ the mass of the adsorbent, and $P$ the pressure. Constants $k$ and $n$ (with $n > 1$) characterize the adsorbent-adsorbate system.

Comparing with the options: Option A matches the Freundlich isotherm exactly. Option B erroneously inverts the ratio $\frac{x}{m}$ to $\frac{m}{x}$. Option C uses an exponent of $n$ instead of $\frac{1}{n}$, and option D combines both errors.

The correct representation is $\boxed{A}$.

60840.text: Argument of the complex number $\mathrm{z}=\frac{13-5 \mathrm{i}}{4-9 \mathrm{i}}, i=\sqrt{-1}$ is
60840.sol:
The complex number $z = \frac{13 - 5i}{4 - 9i}$ is simplified by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, $4 + 9i$.

For the numerator: $(13 - 5i)(4 + 9i) = 52 + 117i - 20i - 45i^2 = 52 + 97i + 45 = 97 + 97i$

The denominator simplifies to: $(4 - 9i)(4 + 9i) = 16 + 81 = 97$

Thus, $z = \frac{97 + 97i}{97} = 1 + i$

The argument is given by $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{Im}(z)}{\text{Re}(z)} = \frac{1}{1} = 1$. Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant, the principal argument is $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\frac{\pi}{4}}$

61267.subject: Mathematics
61267.text: The solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x + y}$, when $x = 0$ and $y = 0$ represents ....
61267.sol:
The given differential equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x - y}{x + y}$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$(x + y)dy = (x - y)dx$

$x dy + y dy = x dx - y dx$

$x dy + y dx = x dx - y dy$

This can be written as exact differentials:

$d(xy) = x dx - y dy$

Integrating both sides, we get:

$\int d(xy) = \int x dx - \int y dy$

$xy = \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{y^2}{2} + C$

$x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = -2C$

Given that $x = 0$ when $y = 0$, substituting these values gives:

$0^2 - 2(0)(0) - 0^2 = -2C \Rightarrow C = 0$

Substituting $C = 0$ back into the equation, we obtain:

$x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = 0$

This is a homogeneous equation of degree 2 in $x$ and $y$ (of the form $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$), which represents a pair of straight lines passing through the origin.

Answer: Pair of straight Lines

61691.subject: Mathematics
61691.text: If $\mathrm{f}(x)=\frac{\sin ^2 x}{1+\cot x}+\frac{\cos ^2 x}{1+\tan x}$, then the value of $\mathrmf^{\prime}  \left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)is equal to$
61691.sol:
Simplify the function:
$\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{\sin^2 x}{1+\cot x} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{1+\tan x}$. Express $\cot x$ and $\tan x$ in terms of sine and cosine:

$\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{\sin^2 x}{1 + \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{1 + \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}} = \frac{\sin^2 x}{\frac{\sin x + \cos x}{\sin x}} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{\frac{\sin x + \cos x}{\cos x}} = \frac{\sin^3 x}{\sin x + \cos x} + \frac{\cos^3 x}{\sin x + \cos x}$.

Combine terms:

$\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{\sin^3 x + \cos^3 x}{\sin x + \cos x}$.

Apply the sum of cubes identity:

$\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{(\sin x + \cos x)(\sin^2 x - \sin x \cos x + \cos^2 x)}{\sin x + \cos x}$.

Cancel the common factor (valid for $\sin x + \cos x \neq 0$):

$\mathrm{f}(x) = \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x - \sin x \cos x = 1 - \sin x \cos x$.

Use the double angle identity $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x \cos x$:

$\mathrm{f}(x) = 1 - \frac{1}{2} \sin(2x)$.

Differentiate:
$\mathrm{f}'(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \left(1 - \frac{1}{2} \sin(2x)\right) = -\frac{1}{2} \cdot \cos(2x) \cdot 2 = -\cos(2x)$.

Evaluate at $x = \frac{\pi}{6}$:

$\mathrm{f}'\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}$.

The correct option is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

62593.text: If $0 \lt x \lt 1$, then $\sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\left\{x \cos \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)+\sin \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)\right\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is equal to
62593.sol:
Let $\cot ^{-1} x=\theta$, then $x=\cot \theta$ and $\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2} \quad \ldots[\because 0 < x < 1 \Rightarrow 0 < \cot \theta < 1] \\
\therefore \quad & \sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\left\{x \cos \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)+\sin \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)\right\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
= & \sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\{\cot \theta \cos \theta+\sin \theta\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
= & \sqrt{1+x^2} \cdot\left\{\left(\frac{\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta}{\sin \theta}\right)^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
= & \sqrt{1+x^2} \sqrt{\operatorname{cosec}^2 \theta-1} \\
= & \sqrt{1+x^2}|\cot \theta| \\
= & \left(\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)|x| \\
= & x \sqrt{1+x^2}
\end{aligned}\ldots[\because 0 < x < 1]$

62725.subject: Mathematics
62725.text: If $\mathrm{f}(x)=\frac{\sin \left(\pi \cos ^2 x\right)}{3 x^2}, x \neq 0$ is continuous at $x=0$ then $\mathrm{f}(0)=$
62725.sol:
To ensure continuity at $x = 0$, we require $\mathrm{f}(0) = \lim_{x \to 0} \mathrm{f}(x)$, where $\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{\sin \left(\pi \cos^2 x\right)}{3 x^2}$ for $x \neq 0$.

Rewriting using $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$, the argument becomes $\pi \cos^2 x = \pi (1 - \sin^2 x) = \pi - \pi \sin^2 x$. Using the identity $\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin \theta$, we have $\sin(\pi \cos^2 x) = \sin(\pi \sin^2 x)$.

The limit evaluates as:

$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\pi \sin^2 x)}{3 x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0} \left[ \frac{\sin(\pi \sin^2 x)}{\pi \sin^2 x} \cdot \frac{\pi \sin^2 x}{3 x^2} \right]

Applying standard limits: as $ x \to 0$, \pi \sin^2 x \to 0$, so the first factor tends to 1.
The second factor simplifies to $\frac{\pi}{3} \left( \frac{\sin x}{x} \right)^2 → \frac{\pi}{3}$.

Therefore, $\mathrm{f}$(0) = $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

$\boxed{\frac{\pi}{3}}$

65104.text: If a vector $3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ is rotated through a certain angle about the origin in the anti-clockwise direction, then the components of the new vector are $a + 1, -3, 5$. The possible values of $a$ is
65104.sol:
When a vector is rotated about the origin, its magnitude remains unchanged.

Let the initial vector be $\vec{v}_1 = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$.

Magnitude of $\vec{v}_1$ is $|\vec{v}_1| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 25} = \sqrt{50}$.

Let the new vector be $\vec{v}_2 = (a+1)\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$.

Magnitude of $\vec{v}_2$ is $|\vec{v}_2| = \sqrt{(a+1)^2 + (-3)^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{(a+1)^2 + 9 + 25} = \sqrt{(a+1)^2 + 34}$.

Since $|\vec{v}_1| = |\vec{v}_2|$, we have:

$\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{(a+1)^2 + 34}

Squaring both sides:

50 = (a+1)^2 + 34$

$(a+1)^2 = 16$

$a+1 = \pm 4$

$a = 3$ or $a = -5$

Answer: -5 or 3

66071.text: Three capacitors each of capacitance 'C' and breakdown voltage 'V' are connected in series. The capacitance and breakdown voltage of the series combination will be respectively
66071.sol:
Equivalent capacitance in series: The reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance $C_{eq}$ equals the sum of reciprocals: $\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{C} = \frac{3}{C}$, so $C_{eq} = \frac{C}{3}$.

Breakdown voltage in series: Voltages across each capacitor add, so the total breakdown voltage is $V_{total} = V + V + V = 3V$.

The combination therefore has capacitance $\frac{C}{3}$ and breakdown voltage $3V$, corresponding to option D.

66820.subject: Physics
66820.text: The magnetic flux through a coil is $4 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ Wb}$ at time $\mathrm{t}=0$. It reduces to $30 \%$ of its original value in time $t$ second. If e.m.f. induced in the coil is 0.56 mV then the value of $t$ is
66820.sol:
The magnetic flux through the coil at t = 0 is $\Phi_1 = 4 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$, which reduces to $30\%$ of its initial value, giving $\Phi_2 = 0.30 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

The change in flux is $\Delta\Phi = \Phi_2 - \Phi_1 = -2.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

Using Faraday's law, $\varepsilon = -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, and the given $\varepsilon = 0.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$, we substitute:

$0.56 \times 10^{-3} = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{t}$

Solving for t, $t = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.56 \times 10^{-3}} = 5 \times 10^{-1} = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

or $\quad \mathrm{mgh}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2$
or $\quad \mathrm{mgh}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \omega^2+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} m r^2\right) \omega^2=\frac{3}{4}{m r^2 \omega^2}^2$
or $\quad \omega^2=\frac{4 \mathrm{gh}}{3 \mathrm{r}^2}$
Now the rotational kinetic energy $=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2\therefore \quad$ Substituting for $\omega^2$ and I , we have,
$\begin{aligned}
\text{ Rotational kinetic energy } & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mr}^2\right) \frac{4 \mathrm{gh}}{3 \mathrm{r}^2} \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{Mgh}}{3}
\end{aligned}$
... $(\because \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m})$

69950.subject: Physics
69950.text: During the isothermal expansion, a confined ideal gas does (-150) J of work against its surroundings. This means that
options: 150 J of heat has been added to the gas
150 J of heat has been removed from the gas
300 J of heat has been added to the gas
no heat is transferred because the process is isothermal
69950.sol:
The First Law of Thermodynamics is expressed as $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $\Delta U$ is the change in internal energy, $Q$ is the heat added to the system, and $W$ is the work done by the system.

Given that the system performs work against its surroundings of magnitude $150\text{ J}$, $W = 150\text{ J}$.

Since the process is isothermal and involves an ideal gas, the internal energy remains constant, so $\Delta U = 0$.

Substituting into the first law: $0 = Q - 150\text{ J}$, which yields $Q = 150\text{ J}$. Thus, the heat added is $150\text{ J}$, and the correct choice is A.

71043.subject: Biology
71043.text: Which one of the following processes does NOT help in nutrient cycling?
71043.sol:
Nutrient cycling involves the movement and exchange of organic and inorganic matter back into the production of living matter. The processes involved include biological, geological, and chemical pathways.

Photosynthesis and respiration are fundamental biological processes that drive the carbon cycle by fixing and releasing carbon dioxide, respectively.

Decomposition is crucial for breaking down complex organic matter into simpler inorganic nutrients, returning them to the soil or atmosphere, thus driving the cycling of elements like carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus.

Evaporation is a physical process that drives the water cycle (hydrological cycle) by converting liquid water into water vapour. It does not play a direct role in the cycling of mineral nutrients.

Answer: Evaporation

71670.subject: Chemistry
71670.text: Why does fructose reduce Fehling's solution?
options: Due to the presence of hydroxy group.
Due to the presence of aldehydic group
Due to the presence of ketonic group.
Due to the presence of alpha-hydroxy ketonic group
71670.sol:
Fructose is a monosaccharide containing a ketonic group at the second carbon and hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, making it an $\alpha$-hydroxy ketone.

Under the alkaline conditions of Fehling's solution, fructose undergoes Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein rearrangement.

This rearrangement converts the $\alpha$-hydroxy ketone into an enediol intermediate, which further tautomerizes into an aldose (a mixture of glucose and mannose).

The newly formed aldehydic group then readily reduces Fehling's solution.

Thus, fructose reduces Fehling's solution due to the presence of the $\alpha$-hydroxy ketonic group.

Answer: Due to the presence of alpha-hydroxy ketonic group

71702.subject: Chemistry
71702.text: Identify a hydride with highest boiling point from following?
71702.sol:
The hydrides of Group 16 elements are $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$, and $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$.

Generally, the boiling point of hydrides increases down the group due to an increase in molecular mass and van der Waals forces. However, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has an exceptionally high boiling point due to the presence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which is absent in the other hydrides.

The order of boiling points is $\text{H}_2\text{S} < \text{H}_2\text{Se} < \text{H}_2\text{Te} < \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Thus, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has the highest boiling point.

Answer: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$

71888.subject: Chemistry
71888.text: Dissociation constant values for $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, HCN, and HF are $4.3 \times 10^{-7}$, $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$, $4.0 \times 10^{-10}$ and $7.2 \times 10^{-4}$ respectively, at $25^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$. Identify the correct order of their increasing acid strength.
71888.sol:
Acid strength is directly proportional to the dissociation constant $K_a$.

Given $K_a$ values are:
$K_a(\text{HCN}) = 4.0 \times 10^{-10}$
$K_a(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3) = 4.3 \times 10^{-7}$
$K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$
$K_a(\text{HF}) = 7.2 \times 10^{-4}$

Arranging the $K_a$ values in increasing order:
$4.0 \times 10^{-10} < 4.3 \times 10^{-7} < 1.8 \times 10^{-5} < 7.2 \times 10^{-4}$

Therefore, the increasing order of acid strength is:
$\text{HCN} < \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} < \text{HF}$

Answer: $\text{HCN} < \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 < \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} < \text{HF}$

71952.subject: Chemistry
71952.text: Which of the following ionic crystals exhibits Schottky defect?
71952.sol:
Schottky defect is a type of point defect that occurs when equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their regular lattice sites, creating vacancies. This defect is typically observed in highly ionic compounds where the cations and anions are of similar sizes and the crystal has a high coordination number.

Sodium chloride (NaCl) satisfies these conditions, as the sizes of $Na^{+}$ and $Cl^{-}$ ions are comparable, and it exhibits a Schottky defect.

In contrast, Silver chloride (AgCl), Silver iodide (AgI), and Calcium fluoride (CaF_2$) have a large difference in the sizes of their cations and anions, which leads them to exhibit Frenkel defects instead.

Answer: Sodium chloride$

72417.subject: Physics
72417.text: Assuming the Sun to be a perfectly spherical black body of radius $R$ and is at a temperature $T\ \text{K}$, then the total radiant power incident on the Earth at a distance $r$ from the sun is ( consider $R_o$ is the radius of the Earth and $\sigma$ is Stefan's constant).
72417.sol:
The total power radiated by the Sun is given by Stefan's law:

$P = \sigma A T^4 = \sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4$

The intensity of this radiation at a distance $r$ from the Sun is:

$I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4}{4\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\sigma R^2 T^4}{r^2}$

The Earth intercepts this radiation over its cross-sectional area, which is $\pi R_o^2$.

The total radiant power incident on the Earth is:

$P_{incident} = I \times \pi R_o^2 = \dfrac{\pi R^2 R_o^2 \sigma T^4}{r^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi R^2 R_o^2 \sigma T^4}{r^2}$

72440.subject: Physics
72440.text: Which of the following is NOT a correct equation for adiabatic process?
72440.sol:
For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic process, the fundamental relationship between pressure ($P$) and volume ($V$) is given by:

$PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$

Using the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT$, we can express volume as $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$. Substituting this into the adiabatic equation:

$P \left( \dfrac{nRT}{P} \right)^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$

$P \cdot P^{-\gamma} \cdot T^{\gamma} = \dfrac{\text{constant}}{(nR)^{\gamma}}$

$P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$

This confirms that $P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ is a valid equation for an adiabatic process, which corresponds to option (3).

Similarly, we can substitute $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$ into the original equation:

$\left( \dfrac{nRT}{V} \right) V^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$

$T V^{\gamma-1} = \dfrac{\text{constant}}{nR} = \text{constant}$

This confirms that $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}$ is also valid, which corresponds to option (2).

Option (4) states $P^{\gamma-1}T^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}$, which contradicts the derived relation $P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$. Therefore, option (4) is NOT a correct equation for an adiabatic process.

Answer: $P^{\gamma-1}T^{\gamma-1} = constant$

72488.subject: Physics
72488.text: The ends of the stretched wire of length L are fixed at $x = 0$ and $x = L$. In one experiment, the displacement of the wire is $y_1 = A\sin \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right) and energy is $E_1$. In another experiment, its displacement is $y_2 = A\sin $\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}\right)$ and energy is $E_2$. Then.
72488.sol:
The total energy of a standing wave in a stretched string is equal to its maximum potential energy, given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{2} T \int_0^L \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^$2 dx$

For the first displacement $y_1 = A\sin$\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right):

\dfrac{dy_1}{dx} = \dfrac{A\pi}{L}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right)$

$E_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} T \int_0^L \dfrac{A^2\pi^2}{L^2}\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right) dx$

Since $\int_0^L \cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right) dx = \dfrac{L}{2}$:

$E_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} T \left(\dfrac{A^2\pi^2}{L^2}\right) \dfrac{L}{2} = \dfrac{T A^2 \pi^2}{4L}$

For the second displacement $y_2 = A\sin $\$left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}\right)$$:

$$\dfrac{dy_2}{dx} = \dfrac{2A\pi}{L}\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}\right)$

$E_2 = $$\dfrac{1}{2}$$T \int_0^L $$\dfrac{4A^2\pi^2}{L^2}\cos^$$2 $\$left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}\right)$$dx$

Since $\int_0^L \$cos^2 $\$left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{L}\right)$$dx = $$\dfrac{L}{2}$:

$E_2 = $$\dfrac{1}{2}$$T $\$left(\dfrac{4A^2\pi^2}{L^2}\right) \dfrac{L}{2} =$4 \$left(\dfrac{T A² \pi^2}{4L}\right)$$

Therefore, $E_2 = 4E_1$.

Answer: $E_2 = 4E_1$

78178.subject: Mathematics
78178.text: If the highest degree coefficient is equal to $1$, then what is the total number of quadratic equations which are unchanged on squaring their roots ?
78178.sol:
Let the quadratic equation be $x^2 + px + q = 0$.

Let its roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Sum of roots: $\alpha + \beta = -p$

Product of roots: $\alpha \beta = q$

The roots of the new equation are $\alpha^2$ and $\beta^2$.

Sum of new roots: $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 2\alpha\beta = p^2 - 2q$

Product of new roots: $\alpha^2 \beta^2 = q^2$

Since the equation remains unchanged, the sum and product of the roots must be the same as the original equation.

Therefore, $p^2 - 2q = -p$ and $q^2 = q$.

From $q^2 = q$, we get $q = 0$ or $q = 1$.

Case 1: $q = 0$

Substituting $q = 0$ in $p^2 - 2q = -p$, we get $p^2 = -p \Rightarrow p^2 + p = 0 \Rightarrow p(p + 1) = 0$.

This gives $p = 0$ or $p = -1$.

The corresponding equations are $x^2 = 0$ and $x^2 - x = 0$.

Case 2: $q = 1$

Substituting $q = 1$ in $p^2 - 2q = -p$, we get $p^2 - 2 = -p \Rightarrow p^2 + p - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (p + 2)(p - 1) = 0$.

This gives $p = -2$ or $p = 1$.

The corresponding equations are $x^2 - 2x + 1 = 0$ and $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$.

Thus, there are $4$ such quadratic equations.

Answer: $4$

91434.text: The locus of the centre of the circle described on any focal chord of the parabola $y^{2} = 4ax$ as the diameter is
91434.sol:
Let, $P\left(a{t}_{1}^{2}, 2a{t}_{1}\right)$ and $Q\left(a{t}_{2}^{2}, 2a{t}_{2}\right)$ be the extremities of a focal chord $PQ$ of the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4ax .$ Then, ${t}_{1}{t}_{2} = - 1 .$
Let, $\left(h, k\right)$ be the coordinates of the centre of the circle described on $PQ$ as diameter. Then,
$h = \dfrac{a}{2}\left({t}_{1}^{2} + {t}_{2}^{2}\right)$ and $k = a\left({t}_{1} + {t}_{2}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{2h}{a} = {t}_{1}^{2} + {t}_{2}^{2}$ and ${\left(\dfrac{k}{a}\right)}^{2} = {\left({t}_{1} + {t}_{2}\right)}^{2}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2h}{a} = {t}_{1}^{2} + {t}_{2}^{2}$ and $\dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = {t}_{1}^{2} + {t}_{2}^{2} + 2{t}_{1}{t}_{2}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = \dfrac{2h}{a} - 2$ $\left[∵ {t}_{1}{t}_{2} = - 1\right]$
$⇒ {k}^{2} = 2a\left(h - a\right)$
Hence, the locus of $\left(h, k\right)$ is
${y}^{2} = 2a\left(x - a\right) .$

91827.text: The sum of $50$ terms of the series $3 + 7 + 13 + 21 + 31 + 43 + . . . . .$ is equal to ${S}_{50}$, then the value of $\dfrac{{S}_{50}}{12500}$ is
91827.sol:
Let, $S = 3 + 7 + 13 + 21 + 31 + 43 + . . . . . + {T}_{n}$
$S = 3 + 7 + 13 + 21 + 31 + . . . . . + {T}_{n - 1} + {T}_{n}$

Subtracting both the equations, we get,

$0 = 3 + \left(4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + . . . . . . . . + \left({T}_{n} - {T}_{n - 1}\right)\right) - {T}_{n}$

$⇒ {T}_{n} = 3 + \left(4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + . . . . . . . . \left(n - 1\right)terms\right) = 3 + \dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)}{2}\left[8 + \left(n - 2\right)2\right]$

$= 3 + \left(n - 1\right)\left(4 + n - 2\right)$

$= 3 + \left(n - 1\right)\left(n + 2\right)$

$= 3 + {n}^{2} + n - 2$

$= {n}^{2} + n + 1$

${S}_{n} = Σ{T}_{n} = Σ{n}^{2} + Σn + Σ1$

$= \dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)}{6} + \dfrac{n\left(n + 1\right)}{2} + n$

If $n = 50,$ ${S}_{50} = \dfrac{50 \times 51 \times 101}{6} + \dfrac{50 \times 51}{2} + 50$

$= 25 \times 17 \times 101 + 25 \times 51 + 50 = 44250$

95277.sol:
In the root of angiospermic plant, the tissue group adjacent to endodermis and towards the central part is called as pericycle. Pericycle generally is composed of parenchymatous cell and in the centre of it lies the pith which is mostly inconspicuous. Formation of lateral root and vascular cambium during the secondary growth occurs at this section.

Epidermis forms the outermost layer of the root having cells giving out root hair in some cells. Phloem is a type of complex vascular tissue which helps in transportation of food throughout the plant.

95320.text:
Arrange the following structures based on their location from the periphery to centre with respect to the anatomy of a dicotyledonous root.
I. Pericycle
II.& Casparian strips
III.& Epiblema
IV. Conjunctive tissue
options: IV, I, II, III
IV, II, III,I
I, II, III, IV
III, II, I, IV
95320.sol: The outermost layer is epiblema. Many of the cells of epiblema protrude in the form of unicellular root hairs. The cortex consists of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma cells, with intercellular spaces. The innermost layer of the cortex is called endodermis. It comprises a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without any intercellular spaces. The tangential, as well as radial walls of the endodermal cells, have a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy material suberin in the form of casparian strips. Next to endodermis lies a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells referred to as pericycle. Initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during the secondary growth takes place in these cells. The pith is small or inconspicuous. The parenchymatous cells which lie between the xylem and the phloem are called conjunctive tissue.

97951.sol:
The negative pressure difference formed between two points that enables flow of gas or liquid to a lower state from higher state is called suction pressure.

The pressure that enables entry of water into the cell due to osmosis is the osmotic pressure (OP) and it is considered negative. The pressure developed in cell due to entry of water and acting opposite to the OP is called turgor pressure (TP). It is a negative pressure as it resists entry of water in cell. The difference between these two results in diffusion pressure deficit (DPD) that equates to the suction pressure. It is directly proportional to the height of the plant/tree.

102797.subject: Physics
102797.text:
Consider the following statements regarding a system of point charges and electric fields:
Statement-I: The electric field due to a point charge decreases as the square of the distance from the charge.
Statement-II: The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point without acceleration.
Statement-III: The net electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charges enclosed within the surface, irrespective of the charges outside.
Statement-IV: The electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is always zero.
Choose the correct option:
options: Statement-I, Statement-II, and Statement-IV are true; Statement-III is false.
Statement-I, Statement-III, and Statement-IV are true; Statement-II is false.
Statement-II and Statement-IV are true; Statement-I and Statement-III are false.
102797.sol:
- Statement-I: This is true. The electric field \(E\) due to a point charge follows the inverse-square law:
\(E=\frac{k q}{r^2}\)
- Statement-II: This is true. The electric potential at a point in space is defined as the work done per unit charge in moving a positive test charge from infinity to that point in an electric field without any acceleration.
- Statement-III: This is true. According to Gauss's Law, the net electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to the charge enclosed within the surface. External charges do not affect the net flux.
- Statement-IV: This is true. In a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the conductor is zero because free charges rearrange themselves on the surface to cancel any internal field.

102877.subject: Physics
102877.text:
Match List-I with List-II for a charged solid spherical conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.

List-IList-II
A. Electric field insideI. $\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$
B. Electrostatic potential insideII. Perpendicular to the surface
C. Electric field magnitude at surfaceIII. Zero
D. Direction of electric field at surfaceIV. Constant (non-zero)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
102877.sol:
In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero (A $\rightarrow$ III).

Because the electric field is zero inside, the electrostatic potential is constant throughout the volume and equals the value on the surface (B $\rightarrow$ IV).

The magnitude of the electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$ (C $\rightarrow$ I).

The direction of the electric field at the surface must be perpendicular to the surface; otherwise, a tangential component would cause charges to move, violating electrostatic equilibrium (D $\rightarrow$ II).

Therefore, the correct match is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Answer: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

103129.subject: Physics
103129.text: Five identical air-filled capacitors, each of capacitance $C$, are connected to form a Wheatstone bridge network between two terminals $A$ and $B$. The equivalent capacitance of this initial network is $C_0$. A dielectric material of dielectric constant $K = 4$ is then completely filled into the two capacitors that are directly connected to terminal $A$. What is the ratio of the new equivalent capacitance of the network to the original equivalent capacitance $C_0$?
103129.sol:
Initially, the five identical capacitors form a balanced Wheatstone bridge. The central capacitor is ineffective, and the equivalent capacitance is $C_0 = \dfrac{C \times C}{C + C} + \dfrac{C \times C}{C + C} = \dfrac{C}{2} + \dfrac{C}{2} = C$.

When a dielectric of $K = 4$ is introduced into the two capacitors connected to terminal $A$, their capacitances become $4C$.
Let the arms connected to terminal $A$ be $C_1 = 4C$ and $C_2 = 4C$.
Let the arms connected to terminal $B$ be $C_3 = C$ and $C_4 = C$.

The ratio of the adjacent arms is $\dfrac{C_1}{C_3} = \dfrac{4C}{C} = 4$ and $\dfrac{C_2}{C_4} = \dfrac{4C}{C} = 4$.
Since $\dfrac{C_1}{C_3} = \dfrac{C_2}{C_4}$, the bridge remains balanced. The central capacitor can still be ignored.

The new equivalent capacitance $C_{new}$ consists of two parallel branches, each having a $4C$ and a $C$ capacitor in series.
Capacitance of one branch $= \dfrac{4C \times C}{4C + C} = \dfrac{4C^2}{5C} = 0.8C$.
Since there are two such branches in parallel, $C_{new} = 0.8C + 0.8C = 1.6C$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{C_{new}}{C_0} = \dfrac{1.6C}{C} = 1.6$.

Answer: $1.6$

104990.text: Two nuclei have mass numbers $64$ and $125$. Assuming them to be perfect spheres, the ratio of their surface areas is:
104990.sol:
The radius $R$ of a nucleus is related to its mass number $A$ by:
$R = R_{0}A^{\dfrac{1}{3}}$

The ratio of the radii of the two nuclei is:
$\dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} = \left(\dfrac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \left(\dfrac{64}{125}\right)^{\dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

Assuming the nuclei to be perfect spheres, the surface area $S$ is given by $S = 4\pi R^{2}$. Thus, the surface area is proportional to the square of the radius ($S \propto R^{2}$).

The ratio of their surface areas is:
$\dfrac{S_{1}}{S_{2}} = \left(\dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}\right)^{2} = \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{16}{25}$

Answer: $16:25$

105567.subject: Physics
105567.text:
Three metallic surfaces A, B, and C are illuminated by monochromatic light of frequency $
u$. The stopping potentials for the photoelectrons emitted from surfaces A and B are $V_A$ and $V_B$ respectively, where $V_A > V_B > 0$. For surface C, no photoelectric emission is observed. If $
u_A$, $
u_B$, and $
u_C$ are the threshold frequencies for metals A, B, and C respectively, which of the following relations is correct?
105567.sol:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the stopping potential $V$ is given by:

$eV = h u - h u_{th}$

For photoelectric emission to occur, the incident frequency $ u$ must be greater than the threshold frequency $ u_{th}$.

Since surfaces A and B emit photoelectrons, we have $ u > u_A$ and $ u > u_B$.

From the equation, for a given incident frequency $ u$, a larger stopping potential implies a smaller threshold frequency. Since $V_A > V_B$, it follows that $ u_A < u_B$.

For surface C, no photoelectric emission is observed, which means the incident frequency is less than or equal to its threshold frequency: $ u \le u_C$.

Combining these inequalities, we get:

$ u_A < u_B < u \le u_C$

Answer: $ u_A < u_B < u \le u_C$

105894.subject: Chemistry
105894.text:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Hydrocarbon, $1$ mole)List-II (Moles of $O_2$ required for complete combustion)
(A) Ethene(I) $2.5$
(B) Ethyne(II) $3$
(C) Ethane(III) $3.5$
(D) Propane(IV) $5$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
105894.sol:
The general equation for the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon $C_xH_y$ is:

$C_xH_y + \left(x + \dfrac{y}{4}\right)O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \dfrac{y}{2}H_2O$

For $1$ mole of each hydrocarbon:
(A) Ethene ($C_2H_4$): $x=2, y=4$. Moles of $O_2 = 2 + \dfrac{4}{4} = 3$.
(B) Ethyne ($C_2H_2$): $x=2, y=2$. Moles of $O_2 = 2 + \dfrac{2}{4} = 2.5$.
(C) Ethane ($C_2H_6$): $x=2, y=6$. Moles of $O_2 = 2 + \dfrac{6}{4} = 3.5$.
(D) Propane ($C_3H_8$): $x=3, y=8$. Moles of $O_2 = 3 + \dfrac{8}{4} = 5$.

Thus, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Incorrect options often result from confusing the chemical formulas of ethene ($C_2H_4$) and ethane ($C_2H_6$), or ethyne ($C_2H_2$) and ethene ($C_2H_4$).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

109201.subject: Chemistry
109201.text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?

(A) The $pH$ of $1 \times {10}^{– 8}MHCl$ solution is $8$. (B) The conjugate base of ${H}_{2}{PO}^{4 -}$ is ${HPO}_{4}^{2 -}$. (C) ${K}_{w}$ increases with increase in temperature. (D) When a solution of a weak monoprotic acid is titrated against a strong base at half neutralisation point, $pH = \dfrac{1}{2}{pK}_{a}$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
109201.sol:
When concentration of ${H}^{+}$ ion is more than ${10}^{- 7}M$, the proton concentration from water must be considered. Hence, the pH of ${10}^{- 8}MHCl$ solution is not equal to 8.

$\mathop{{H}_{2}{PO}_{4}^{-}}_{Acid}\overset{}{⇌}\mathop{{HPO}_{4}^{2 -}}_{Conjugatebase} + {H}^{+}$

${K}_{w}$ increase with increase in temperature as dissociation of water increases with increase in temperature.

When weak monoprotic acid is titrated against strong base, at half neutralization point, the solution becomes acidic buffer and its $pH$ is given by

$pH = {pK}_{a} + log\dfrac{\left[Salt\right]}{\left[Acid\right]}$

$⇒ pH = {pK}_{a} + 0$ as $\left[salt\right] = \left[acid\right]$

117058.subject: Chemistry
117058.text:
Consider the following oxides of manganese: $\mathrm{MnO}, \mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_3, \mathrm{MnO}_2$, and $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7$.

Identify the acid-base nature of the oxide with the highest oxidation state of manganese, and calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of the manganese ion in the most basic oxide among these.
117058.sol:
The oxidation states of manganese in the given oxides are: $\mathrm{MnO}$ (+2), $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_3$ (+3), $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ (+4), and $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7$ (+7).

As the oxidation state of a transition metal increases, the acidic character of its oxide increases. Therefore, the oxide with the highest oxidation state, $\mathrm{Mn}_2\mathrm{O}_7$, is acidic in nature.

The most basic oxide is the one with the lowest oxidation state, which is $\mathrm{MnO}$ (+2).

In $\mathrm{MnO}$, the manganese ion is $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$. The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3\mathrm{d}^5$.
The number of unpaired electrons ($n$) is 5.
The spin-only magnetic moment ($\mu$) is calculated as:
$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \text{ BM}$.

Thus, the highest oxidation state oxide is acidic, and the magnetic moment of the metal in the most basic oxide is $5.92 \text{ BM}$.

Answer: Acidic, $5.92 \text{ BM}$

119564.subject: Chemistry
119564.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Reaction)List II (Product Property)
(A) $p$-Methoxytoluene + $\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+$(I) Product is a stronger acid than benzoic acid
(B) $p$-Chlorotoluene + $\text{KMnO}_4/\text{H}^+$(II) Product is a weaker acid than benzoic acid
(C) $p$-Nitroanisole + $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$(III) Product is a stronger base than aniline
(D) $p$-Chloronitrobenzene + $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$(IV) Product is a weaker base than aniline

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
119564.sol:
(A) Oxidation of $p$-methoxytoluene with acidic $\text{KMnO}_4$ yields $p$-methoxybenzoic acid. The $-\text{OCH}_3$ group has a strong $+M$ effect which outweighs its $-I$ effect, making the product a weaker acid than benzoic acid. (Matches II)

(B) Oxidation of $p$-chlorotoluene yields $p$-chlorobenzoic acid. For halogens, the $-I$ effect outweighs the $+M$ effect, making the product a stronger acid than benzoic acid. (Matches I)

(C) Reduction of $p$-nitroanisole with $\text{Sn}/\text{HCl}$ yields $p$-anisidine. The $+M$ effect of the $-\text{OCH}_3$ group increases electron density on the nitrogen, making the product a stronger base than aniline. (Matches III)

(D) Reduction of $p$-chloronitrobenzene yields $p$-chloroaniline. The net electron-withdrawing nature of chlorine ($-I > +M$) decreases electron density on the nitrogen, making the product a weaker base than aniline. (Matches IV)

The correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

A black precipitate is formed in the lead acetate test for sulphide. A brown ring is the confirmatory test for nitrate. A yellow precipitate is formed in the confirmatory test for phosphate or arsenic.

Answer: Purple or violet colouration

121769.subject: Botany
121769.text: What is the male sex organ in bryophytes called?
121769.sol: Bryophytes include the various mosses and liverworts that are found commonly growing in moist shaded areas in the hills. Bryophytes are also called amphibians of the plant kingdom because these plants can live in soil but are dependent on water for sexual reproduction. They usually occur in damp, humid and shaded localities. They play an important role in plant succession on bare rocks/soil. The plant body of bryophytes is more differentiated than that of algae. It is thallus-like and prostrate or erect, and attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids. They lack true roots, stems or leaves. They may possess root-like, leaf-like or stem-like structures. The main plant body of the bryophyte is haploid. It produces gametes, hence is called a gametophyte. The sex organs in bryophytes are multicellular. <mark>The male sex organ is called antheridium.</mark>

125004.subject: Botany
125004.text: What is the role of oxygen in the electron transport chain?
125004.sol: Although the aerobic process of respiration takes place only in the presence of oxygen, the role of oxygen is limited to the terminal stage of the process. Yet, the presence of oxygen is vital, since it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system. Oxygen acts as the final hydrogen acceptor. Unlike photophosphorylation where it is the light energy that is utilized for the production of proton gradient required for phosphorylation, in respiration it is the energy of oxidation-reduction utilized for the same process. It is for this reason that the process is called oxidative phosphorylation.

125671.subject: Botany
125671.text: Identify the correct statement regarding the spatial arrangement of complexes and proton accumulation in the thylakoid membrane during light reactions.
options: The water splitting complex is physically located on the outer side of the thylakoid membrane.
The NADP reductase enzyme is located on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane.
During electron transport, protons accumulate in the stroma of the chloroplast.
The primary electron acceptor of PS II is located towards the inner side of the thylakoid membrane.
125671.sol:
According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis in chloroplasts:

The NADP reductase enzyme is located on the stroma side of the membrane. Along with electrons from the acceptor of PS I, protons are necessary for the reduction of $\text{NADP}^+$ to $\text{NADPH} + \text{H}^+$. These protons are removed from the stroma. Thus, this statement is correct.

The water splitting complex is associated with PS II, which is physically located on the inner side of the membrane (lumen side), not the outer side.

During electron transport, protons accumulate in the lumen of the thylakoids, not in the stroma.

The primary electron acceptor of PS II is located towards the outer side of the membrane, not the inner side, and it transfers its electron to an H carrier.

Answer: The NADP reductase enzyme is located on the stroma side of the thylakoid membrane.

127792.subject: Botany
127792.text:
In an aquatic ecosystem, the total rate at which solar energy is captured by phytoplankton during photosynthesis is reduced by the energy utilised for their own respiration. The remaining biomass, which is available for consumption by zooplankton, is termed as 'X' and is typically measured in units of 'Y'.

Select the correct option for X and Y.
options: X = Gross Primary Productivity ; Y = $\mathrm{g \, m}^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$
X = Net Primary Productivity ; Y = $\mathrm{g \, m}^{-2}$
X = Net Primary Productivity ; Y = $\mathrm{kcal \, m}^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$
127792.sol:
The total rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis is called Gross Primary Productivity (GPP).

A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by producers (phytoplankton) in respiration (R). The remaining biomass, which is available for consumption by heterotrophs (like zooplankton), is called Net Primary Productivity (NPP). Thus, NPP = GPP - R.

Since NPP is a rate of production (productivity), it must be expressed with both an area and a time dimension. Its standard units are $\mathrm{g \, m}^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ or $\mathrm{kcal \, m}^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.

The option with Y = $\mathrm{g \, m}^{-2}$ is incorrect because it lacks a time dimension and represents the unit for standing crop, not productivity.

Answer: X = Net Primary Productivity ; Y = $\mathrm{kcal \, m}^{-2} \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$

128132.subject: Zoology
128132.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Gap junctions facilitate rapid communication between adjacent cells in animal tissues.
Reason (R): Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
128132.sol:
Assertion (A) is a true statement because gap junctions facilitate the cells to communicate with each other by connecting the cytoplasm of adjoining cells for rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.

Reason (R) is also a true statement because adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together.

However, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A) as they describe two entirely different types of junctions with distinct physiological roles.

128362.subject: Zoology
128362.text: What is the function of insulin in the body?
128362.sol: Insulin is a peptide hormone, which plays a major role in the regulation of glucose homeostasis. Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes (cells of adipose tissue), and enhances cellular glucose uptake and utilisation. As a result, there is a rapid movement of glucose from blood to hepatocytes and adipocytes resulting in decreased blood glucose levels (hypoglycemia). Insulin also stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) in the target cells. The glucose homeostasis in blood is thus maintained jointly by the two – insulin and glucagons.Prolonged hyperglycemia leads to a complex disorder called diabetes mellitus which is associated with loss of glucose through urine and formation of harmful compounds known as ketone bodies. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy.

129455.subject: Zoology
129455.text: What is the process of excreting ammonia called?
129455.sol: The process of excreting ammonia is Ammonotelism. Many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects are ammonotelic in nature. Ammonia, as it is readily soluble, is generally excreted by diffusion across body surfaces or through gill surfaces (in fish) as ammonium ions. Kidneys do not play any significant role in its removal. Terrestrial adaptation necessitated the production of lesser toxic nitrogenous wastes like urea and uric acid for conservation of water. Mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes mainly excrete urea and are called ureotelic ureotelicureotelic animals. Ammonia produced by metabolism is converted into urea in the liver of these animals and released into the blood which is filtered and excreted out by the kidneys. Some amount of urea may be retained in the kidney matrix of some of these animals to maintain a desired osmolarity. Reptiles, birds, land snails and insects excrete nitrogenous wastes as uric acid in the form of pellet or paste with a minimum loss of water and are called uricotelic animals.
129455.meta: What is the process of excreting ammonia called?

129556.subject: Zoology
129556.text: What mechanism acts as a check on the Renin-Angiotensin mechanism?
129556.sol: he JGA plays a complex regulatory role. A fall in glomerular blood flow/glomerular blood pressure/GFR can activate the JG cells to release renin which converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I and further to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II, being a powerful vasoconstrictor, increases the glomerular blood pressure and thereby GFR. Angiotensin II also activates the adrenal cortex to release Aldosterone. Aldosterone causes reabsorption of Na+ and water from the distal parts of the tubule. This also leads to an increase in blood pressure and GFR. This complex mechanism is generally known as the Renin-Angiotensin mechanism. An increase in blood flow to the atria of the heart can cause the release of Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF). ANF can cause vasodilation (dilation of blood vessels) and thereby decrease the blood pressure. ANF mechanism, therefore, acts as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

129755.subject: Zoology
129755.text: During urine formation, which of the following processes create high osmotic pressure in the uriniferous tubule?
options: Active secretion of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$into efferent arteriole followed by absorption of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$into efferent renal arteriole
Active secretion of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$and absorption of $\mathrm{N}^{+}$a into efferent renal arteriole
129755.sol:
- Active sodium absorption is followed by the absorption of chlorine. Sodium is the positively charged electrolyte in extracellular body fluid. The amount of sodium in the fluid influences its volume, which in turn determines blood volume and blood pressure.
- Most of the sodium is reabsorbed in the form of sodium bicarbonate and sodium chloride.
- About \(70 \%\) of the sodium reabsorption occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule. When sodium ion moves, water follows. The movement of water balances the osmotic pressure within or across the tubule walls, which maintains extracellular fluid volume.
- The fluid entering the late proximal tubule has been depleted of the essential substances. As bicarbonate being negatively charged was reabsorbed initially with sodium, chloride ion has been left behind in the tubule.
- Due to the extensive reabsorption of water in the early part of the tubule, chloride ions are highly concentrated and get reabsorbed. So, the correct option is A.

129859.subject: Zoology
129859.text: In what direction is the gradient present for CO₂ in the body?
129859.sol: gradient is present for CO2 in the opposite direction, i.e., from tissues to blood and blood to alveoli. As the solubility of CO2 is 20-25 times higher than that of O2, the amount of CO2 that can diffuse through the diffusion membrane per unit difference in partial pressure is much higher compared to that of O2. The diffusion membrane is made up of three major layers namely, the thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, the endothelium of alveolar capillaries and the basement substance (composed of a thin basement membrane supporting the squamous epithelium and the basement membrane surrounding the single layer endothelial cells of capillaries) in between them. However, its total thickness is much less than a millimetre. Therefore, all the factors in our body are favourable for diffusion of O2 from alveoli to tissues and that of CO2 from tissues to alveoli.

131235.subject: Zoology
131235.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The ovum released during ovulation is surrounded by the corona radiata.
Reason (R): Corona radiata is an inner non-cellular layer secreted by the oocyte.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
131235.sol:
The Assertion (A) is true because at the time of ovulation, the secondary oocyte (ovum) is released from the Graafian follicle along with its surrounding layers, which include the zona pellucida and the corona radiata.

The Reason (R) is false because the corona radiata is an outer, cellular layer formed by the follicular (granulosa) cells. The inner, non-cellular (acellular) layer secreted by the oocyte is actually the zona pellucida.

Therefore, Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

131435.subject: Zoology
131435.text: What is the function of nucleosomes in chromatin structure?
options: To prevent the entry of pathogens
To wrap around the DNA in nucleosomes
To help organize the DNA into a nucleoid
131435.sol: In eukaryotes, this organization is much more complex. There is a set of positively charged, basic proteins called histones. A protein acquires charge depending upon the abundance of amino acids residues with charged side chains. Histones are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine. Both the amino acid residues carry positive charges in their side chains. Histones are organized to form a unit of eight molecules called histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a structure called nucleosome (Figure 5.4 a). A typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix. Nucleosomes constitute the repeating unit of a structure in the nucleus called chromatin, threadlike stained (coloured) bodies seen in the nucleus. The nucleosomes in chromatin are seen as ‘beads-on-string’ structure when viewed under electron microscope

132692.subject: Zoology
132692.text: What change was observed in the population of moths before and after industrialization in England?
options: No change in the population of moths
132692.sol: Man has bred selected plants and animals for agriculture, horticulture, sport or security. Man has domesticated many wild animals and crops. This intensive breeding programme has created breeds that differ from other breeds (e.g., dogs) but still are of the same group. It is argued that if within hundreds of years, man could create new breeds, could not nature have done the same over millions of years? Another interesting observation supporting evolution by natural selection comes from England. In a collection of moths made in 1850s, i.e., before industrialisation set in, it was observed that there were more white-winged moths on trees than dark-winged or melanised moths. However, in the collection carried out from the same area, but after industrialisation, i.e., in 1920, there were more dark-winged moths in the same area, i.e., the proportion was reversed

135062.subject: Zoology
135062.text: How is the tiger census in national parks and reserves often conducted?
options: By using pug marks and fecal pellets
135062.sol: Although total number is generally the most appropriate measure of population density, it is in some cases either meaningless or difficult to determine. In an area, if there are 200 carrot grass (Parthenium hysterophorus) plants but only a single huge banyan tree with a large canopy, stating that the population density of banyan is low relative to that of carrot grass amounts to underestimating the enormous role of the Banyan in that community. In such cases, the percent cover or biomass is a more meaningful measure of the population size. Total number is again not an easily adoptable measure if the population is huge and counting is impossible or very time-consuming. If you have a dense laboratory culture of bacteria in a petri dish what is the best measure to report its density? Sometimes, for certain ecological investigations, there is no need to know the absolute population densities; relative densities serve the purpose equally well. For instance, the number of fish caught per trap is a good enough measure of its total population density in the lake. We are mostly obliged to estimate population sizes indirectly, without actually counting them or seeing them. <mark>The tiger census in our national parks and tiger reserves is often based on pug marks and fecal pellets.</mark>
